title: Values & Character
description: Character and values drawn from many traditions and from universal human experience: honesty, kindness, courage, fairness, responsibility, gratitude, perseverance, humility, integrity and justice. Children explore values through stories and real choices, and learn to reason about dilemmas.

lessons.title: The Broken Vase
objectives: Explain why telling the truth matters
Practise owning up to a mistake
explanation: Being honest means telling the truth. When we tell the truth, people can trust us — they believe what we say.
Sometimes telling the truth is hard, especially when we've made a mistake. But owning up ("I did it, I'm sorry") is brave, and it helps fix the problem.
Everyone makes mistakes. Grown-ups usually feel proud when children are honest, even about mistakes.

vocabulary.meaning: something that went wrong by accident

examples: "I spilled the milk. Sorry! I'll help clean it."
Giving back extra change a shopkeeper gave by mistake.

story.title: The Broken Pot
story.text: Kiko was playing ball indoors and — crash! — Grandma's clay pot broke. Kiko wanted to hide. But Kiko took a deep breath and went to Grandma. "I broke your pot. I'm really sorry." Grandma hugged Kiko. "I'm sad about the pot, but I'm proud you told the truth. Let's make a new one together."

activities.prompt: If you break something by accident, you should…
Owning up to a mistake is brave.

thinking: Why might someone tell a lie?
How do you feel after telling the truth about a mistake?
speaking: Tell a grown-up about a time you told the truth even though it was hard.

lessons.title: Little Acts of Kindness
objectives: Do and describe kind acts
Notice how kindness makes others and ourselves feel
explanation: Kindness means caring about others and doing things to help or make them happy — without expecting anything back.
Kind acts can be small: helping set the table, sharing a snack, drawing a picture for Grandpa, watering plants, or filling a water bowl for birds.
Kindness feels good for the person receiving it and the person giving it. It spreads, too — one kind act can inspire another.
examples: Holding the door for someone carrying bags.
Comforting a friend who is sad.

story.title: The Kindness Chain
story.text: Momo shared an umbrella with Tara in the rain. Tara felt so happy that she helped Zuri carry her books. Zuri then gave Kiko a mango. Kiko drew a picture for Grandma Owl. "One kind act," hooted Olu, "and look how far it travelled!"

lessons.title: Is It Fair?
objectives: Explain what fairness means
Understand that fair doesn't always mean exactly the same
explanation: Being fair means treating people justly — giving everyone a fair chance and following the rules.
Sometimes fair means equal: everyone gets the same number of sweets. But sometimes fair means giving people what they need: a child who can't see well sits at the front.
Cheating is unfair because it breaks the rules and takes away others' fair chance.
examples: Sharing a roti into equal pieces.
Giving extra help to a friend who has a hurt arm.

story.title: The Fence and the Mangoes
story.text: Three friends of different heights wanted to see over a fence to the mango festival. Giving each one box (equal) still left the smallest unable to see. Giving boxes by need — none for the tallest, two for the smallest — let everyone see. "That's fair," said Zuri.

explanation: Responsibility means doing your jobs and taking care of things: tidying toys, feeding a pet, packing your school bag, keeping promises.
When we are responsible, people can count on us — and we feel proud and grown-up.
Gratitude means noticing good things and saying thank you — to people who help us, for food, for nature. Grateful people often feel happier.

story.text: Rangi was given the job of watering the class plant. For a week, Rangi forgot, and the leaves drooped. Rangi felt bad, made a reminder picture, and watered it every day after. The plant grew a flower! Rangi thanked the class for trusting a chameleon with such an important job.

lessons.title: Brave Choices
objectives: Describe different kinds of courage
Identify courageous choices in daily life
explanation: Courage means doing the right or important thing even when you feel scared. Being brave doesn't mean having no fear — it means acting despite it.
Physical courage might be learning to swim. Moral courage is standing up for what's right: telling the truth, speaking up for someone being teased, or saying no to something wrong.
Small brave acts count: trying a new food, raising your hand to answer, saying sorry first.

vocabulary.meaning: standing up for what is right

examples: Speaking up when a friend is being teased.
Trying again after falling off a bicycle.

story.title: Malala's Voice
story.text: As a girl in Pakistan's Swat Valley, Malala Yousafzai spoke out for girls' right to go to school, even when this was dangerous. She was attacked in 2012 but survived and continued her campaign. In 2014, she became the youngest person to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, sharing it with India's Kailash Satyarthi, who campaigns against child labour.

options: doing the right thing even when scared
standing up for someone being teased

pairs: telling the truth when it's hard

lessons.title: The Mountain Man
objectives: Explain perseverance
Use strategies to keep going on hard tasks
explanation: Perseverance means continuing to try even when something is hard or takes a long time.
Strategies: break the task into small steps, take short breaks, ask for help, and remember how far you've already come.
Patience goes with perseverance — some things simply take time, like growing a plant or learning to read.

context.text: Dashrath Manjhi of Gehlaur, Bihar, spent about 22 years (roughly 1960–1982) carving a path through a hill with hand tools, shortening the route to the nearest town.

examples: Practising a song every day until you can play it.

story.title: The Man Who Moved a Mountain
story.text: In a village in Bihar, Dashrath Manjhi lived on one side of a rocky hill, far from the nearest town and hospital. After his wife was badly injured crossing it, he began to cut a path through the hill with only a hammer and chisel. People laughed. He kept going for about 22 years — and made a road that saved his neighbours hours of travel.

lessons.title: When No One Is Watching
objectives: Define integrity
Reason through situations that test integrity
explanation: Integrity means being honest and doing what's right consistently — even when no one is watching and you could get away with something.
It means your actions match your words: if you say you value fairness, you play fairly even when the referee isn't looking.
Integrity is tested by temptation. Pausing to ask "Would I be proud if everyone knew?" helps.

vocabulary.meaning: being honest and doing right consistently

examples: Returning a lost wallet with all the money inside.
Not copying answers in a test even when the teacher steps out.

lessons.title: The Golden Rule
objectives: Identify the Golden Rule in several traditions
Explain how shared values can unite people with different beliefs
explanation: Many religious and philosophical traditions teach a version of the Golden Rule: treat others as you would like to be treated.

It appears in Confucius ("Do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself"), the Mahabharata (a teaching not to do to others what would be painful to oneself), the Bible ("Do to others as you would have them do to you"), and sayings attributed to the Prophet Muhammad and in Jewish teaching.
Traditions also emphasise values like ahimsa (non-violence), seva (service), compassion and charity. Different beliefs can share common values, which helps people live together respectfully.

context.text: Each tradition expresses the Golden Rule within its own beliefs and texts; followers understand it in the context of their faith.
Scholars note that versions differ (positive "do" and negative "do not" forms), and traditions add their own emphases.

vocabulary.meaning: treat others as you want to be treated
beliefs and practices passed down through generations

examples: Not spreading a rumour because you wouldn't want one spread about you.
Helping a neighbour as you'd hope to be helped.

story.title: The Interfaith Kitchen
story.text: During a flood, people from a temple, a mosque, a church and a gurdwara cooked together in one community kitchen. Volunteers had different prayers and festivals, but all said the same thing when asked why they came: "We would want someone to help us."

thinking: Is the Golden Rule always enough? What if someone wants to be treated differently from you?

speaking: Share a version of the Golden Rule from a tradition you know and explain it.

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: Three Ways to Think About Right and Wrong
objectives: Apply consequence, duty and virtue approaches to a dilemma
Recognise that thoughtful people can disagree
explanation: A moral dilemma is a situation where values clash: being honest might hurt a friend's feelings; keeping a promise might mean not helping someone else.

Philosophers offer different lenses. Consequences: which choice produces the best results for everyone? Duties: what rules or duties apply (tell the truth, keep promises)? Virtues: what would a good, kind, honest person do?

Indian thought also discusses dharma — duty and right action — which can depend on one's role and situation, as explored in the Mahabharata and Bhagavad Gita. Using several lenses helps us reason carefully, even when we disagree.

context.text: Consequentialism, deontology (duty ethics) and virtue ethics are major Western philosophical frameworks; Indian traditions discuss dharma in varied and debated ways. These are tools for reasoning, not a single correct answer.

vocabulary.meaning: a difficult choice between conflicting values

examples: A friend asks if you like their drawing, and you don't.
You promised to meet a friend but find someone who needs help.

story.title: The Promise and the Stranger
story.text: Arun promised to meet his friend at 5 pm. On the way, he saw an elderly man who had fallen and needed help getting home. Helping would make Arun late. He thought: the consequences (the man could be hurt), his duty (his promise), and what a kind person would do. He helped, then called his friend to explain. His friend understood.

pairs: Which choice has the best results?
What would a good person do?

activities.prompt: Thoughtful people can reach different conclusions on dilemmas.
Dharma in Indian thought relates to…

thinking: Is it ever right to break a promise?
Which lens do you find most convincing, and why?
speaking: Present a dilemma to your family, analysing it through all three lenses.

project.title: Dilemma Discussion Circle
steps: Write five realistic dilemmas

Write a reflection on what you learned about reasoning

lessons.title: Equality, Equity and Justice
objectives: Distinguish equality from equity
Describe contributions of justice reformers
explanation: Equality means treating everyone the same. Equity means giving people what they need to have fair opportunities, recognising that people start from different places.

Justice involves fair laws and fair treatment for all. In India, Dr B. R. Ambedkar, chair of the Constitution's drafting committee, championed equality and fought against caste discrimination; the Constitution abolished untouchability (Article 17).
Reformers across history — such as Savitribai Phule, who opened schools for girls in the 1840s, and Raja Ram Mohan Roy — challenged injustice. Justice is an ongoing project for every generation.

context.text: Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848. Article 17 of the Constitution of India abolishes untouchability.

vocabulary.meaning: unfair treatment because of who someone is

examples: Ramps (equity) let wheelchair users enter buildings like everyone else.
Scholarships for students facing disadvantage.

story.title: The Teacher Who Was Pelted
story.text: When Savitribai Phule walked to teach girls in 1840s Pune, some people threw mud and stones at her. She carried a second sari to change into at school. She kept teaching. Today, her birthday, 3 January, is celebrated in Maharashtra and beyond as a tribute to women's education.

pairs: large-print books for a student who needs them

lessons.title: Comparing Ethical Theories
objectives: Explain major ethical theories from different traditions
Evaluate strengths and weaknesses of each
explanation: Utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill) judges actions by consequences: the right action maximises overall well-being. Kantian ethics holds that some actions are right or wrong regardless of consequences; we should act only on principles we could will as universal laws and treat people as ends, never merely as means.

Virtue ethics (Aristotle, and Confucius in a different form) focuses on developing good character — courage, justice, temperance, ren (humaneness). Buddhist ethics emphasises reducing suffering through right intention, speech and action.
The Bhagavad Gita teaches nishkama karma — acting according to one's dharma without attachment to results. Each theory captures something important and faces objections; many people draw on several.

context.text: These are summaries of complex traditions with many internal debates; the Gita's teachings, for example, are interpreted in varied ways by commentators and scholars.

vocabulary.meaning: ethics judging actions by overall consequences
Kant's principle of acting on universalisable rules
action without attachment to its fruits

examples: Utilitarian: a policy that helps the most people.
Kantian: never lying, even with good intentions.

story.title: The Trolley Debate
story.text: A seminar discussed a famous thought experiment: a runaway trolley will hit five people unless you divert it, killing one. Utilitarians said divert it; Kantian-leaning students hesitated to use one person as a means; virtue ethicists asked what a wise, compassionate person would do. The debate showed each theory's insights — and limits.

activities.prompt: Match the theory to the thinker
Many people draw on more than one ethical theory.
Kant said people should be treated as…

thinking: Which theory best handles a conflict between honesty and kindness?
Can an action be right if it leads to bad results?
speaking: Present a contemporary dilemma analysed through three theories, then give your view.

project.title: Ethics Essay

lessons.title: Ethics of Technology
objectives: Analyse ethical issues in technology
Propose ethical guidelines
explanation: New technologies raise new ethical questions. AI systems can carry bias from their training data, affecting decisions about jobs, loans or policing. Who is responsible when an automated system causes harm?
Data privacy asks how personal information should be collected and used. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, sets rules for handling personal data.

Ethical guidelines often include fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy and human oversight. Applying ethical theories helps: What are the consequences? Are people respected? What would a responsible designer do?

context.text: Studies have documented bias in some facial recognition and hiring algorithms, with higher error rates for certain groups.

vocabulary.meaning: being open about how decisions are made

examples: A hiring algorithm favouring one group because of biased historical data.
Apps asking for more permissions than they need.

story.title: The Unfair Filter
story.text: A company built an automated system to sort job applications, trained on past hires. It began rejecting applications from women — because most past hires had been men. Engineers discovered the bias and scrapped the system. "Data reflects the past," one said, "and the past isn't always fair."

activities.prompt: India passed a Digital Personal Data Protection Act in 2023.

options: people can review and correct automated decisions

thinking: Should AI ever make decisions about people without human review?
Who should be responsible when technology causes harm?
speaking: Debate a technology ethics question, presenting at least two perspectives fairly.

project.title: Ethical Design Charter
steps: Choose an app or technology
Identify ethical risks (bias, privacy, safety)

Present it with examples

assessment.prompt: Ethical theories can help analyse technology issues.
